Algorithm Deep-Dive

How the Affine Motion Segmentation Processor Works

A comprehensive walkthrough of the algorithm — from affine models and weighted least-squares estimation, through MRF-based boundary update and region detection, to the pixel-pipeline innovations that achieve real-time VGA 91 fps on a single VLSI chip.

Miyama & Matsuda · Kanazawa Univ. IEICE 2014 0.18 µm CMOS VGA 91 fps
01 — Overview

What Is Motion Segmentation?

Motion segmentation takes two consecutive video frames and partitions the image into regions whose pixels share the same motion pattern. Each region receives a unique label, and the collection of pixel labels forms a label map. For example, if a car moves left while the background scrolls right, the algorithm produces two labels — one for the car and one for the background — even though the raw pixel data looks like a single blended image.

Motion segmentation approaches fall into two broad categories. Top-down hierarchical methods compute the dominant motion of the entire image, assign matching pixels, then repeat for the remainder — but accuracy degrades as regions shrink. Clustering methods compute optical flow for every pixel and group similar vectors — but results depend heavily on a predetermined cluster count. This processor takes a top-down approach but avoids its weakness through weighted iterative least-squares, which cleanly isolates each region's dominant motion even when outliers are present.

The Affine Motion Model

Instead of storing per-pixel flow vectors, each region's motion is compactly described by six affine parameters:

θ = (a₁ a₂ a₃ a₄ a₅ a₆)

These six numbers can express translation, rotation, and scaling. Given a pixel at position (xᵢ, yᵢ), its displacement (uᵢ, vᵢ) between frame I(t) and frame I(t+1) is:

uᵢ = a₁ + a₂·xᵢ + a₃·yᵢ vᵢ = a₄ + a₅·xᵢ + a₆·yᵢ // u = horizontal displacement, v = vertical displacement

The parameter meanings are intuitive: a₁ and a₄ represent constant horizontal and vertical translation. a₂, a₃, a₅, a₆ encode how motion changes with pixel position — encoding rotation and zoom. An additional brightness-change parameter ξ is appended to handle global illumination drift between frames, forming the extended parameter vector θ = (a₁ a₂ a₃ a₄ a₅ a₆ ξ).

Why affine? An affine model is rich enough to describe most rigid-body motion (cars, pedestrians, buildings) yet compact enough to estimate robustly from noisy video. More complex models (projective, polynomial) require more data and are harder to solve in hardware.
Fig. — Motion model estimation example: a scaling motion θ=[0, 0.25, 0, 0, 0, 0.25]ᵀ applied to a tree image. The gradient field ∇J and displaced frame difference r are used to solve for the incremental update Δd.
02 — Pipeline

The Four-Stage Loop

At time t = 0 the prediction map is initialized (all pixels labeled as background). For each subsequent frame pair, the algorithm executes four stages in order, then feeds its output forward as the starting point for the next pair:

Fig. — The four-stage motion segmentation loop. Each frame pair cycles through all stages; the prediction map feeds forward.

The motion model θ estimated in Step 1 is used in Steps 2, 3, and 4. The label map m(t) produced by Steps 2–3 is the final segmentation output. The prediction map m̃(t+1) from Step 4 initializes the next frame's processing, providing temporal continuity.

03 — Step 1

Motion Model Estimation

The goal is to find, for each labeled region, the seven parameters θ = (a₁ a₂ a₃ a₄ a₅ a₆ ξ) that best describe how pixels in that region moved between frames. This is formulated as a weighted least-squares optimization.

Luminance Gradients

The algorithm relies on the brightness constancy assumption: a pixel's intensity should remain approximately the same after motion. The difference between the current and next frame at the moved position yields the displaced frame difference (DFD). To linearize this into a solvable system, spatial and temporal luminance gradients are computed:

Ix = ∂I/∂x // horizontal spatial gradient Iy = ∂I/∂y // vertical spatial gradient It = ∂I/∂t // temporal gradient (frame difference)

These three gradients are the fundamental building blocks. They are combined with pixel coordinates to form the gradient vector χ for each pixel:

χᵢ = ( Ix xᵢ·Ix yᵢ·Ix Iy xᵢ·Iy yᵢ·Iy 1 ) // 7-element vector per pixel — the last element corresponds to ξ

The temporal gradient input is also derived from these values:

υᵢ = −It // observation vector per pixel

Weighted Least Squares Solution

For region F, define an error function summing the weighted squared residuals of all pixels:

E = Σ ½ · wᵢ · rᵢ² over all (xᵢ,yᵢ) ∈ F

The residual rᵢ represents the brightness mismatch after applying the motion model:

rᵢ = I(xᵢ + uᵢ, yᵢ + vᵢ, t+1) − I(xᵢ, yᵢ, t) + ξ // displaced frame difference including brightness compensation

The weight wᵢ is a binary value (0 or 1) to reject outliers. Minimizing E yields the gradient image moment solution:

θ = G⁻¹ · d where: G = Σ wᵢ · χᵢᵀ · χᵢ // 7×7 symmetric matrix d = Σ wᵢ · χᵢᵀ · υᵢ // 7×1 vector // sums over all pixels (xᵢ,yᵢ) ∈ F

The matrix G is built by accumulating outer products of the gradient vector χ, weighted by wᵢ, across all pixels in the region. Each element of G is a gradient image moment — products like Σ(wᵢ · xᵢ² · Ix²), Σ(wᵢ · xᵢ · yᵢ · Ix · Iy), etc. Because G is symmetric, only 28 unique elements are accumulated. The vector d similarly accumulates gradient-temporal products. Computing G⁻¹ via Gauss-Jordan elimination and multiplying by d gives the optimal motion parameters.

Key insight: Because G and d are accumulated pixel by pixel, this computation naturally maps to a streaming pipeline — each pixel contributes its terms as it arrives, and the matrix inversion happens once at the end of each region.

Outlier Rejection via Motion Accuracy Index

Not all pixels in a region truly belong to it — some are mislabeled from previous frames, or sit on occluded boundaries. Including these outliers would corrupt the motion estimate. The algorithm computes a motion accuracy index qᵢ for every pixel:

Σⱼ |∇Ij| · DFDθ(xj, yj) qᵢ = ───────────────────────────── max( Σⱼ |∇Ij|² , 9·σ² ) // j ∈ N(i) : pixel i and its 8 neighbors (3×3 window) // ∇I = (Ix, Iy)ᵀ = spatial gradient magnitude // σ = assumed noise standard deviation

The DFD (Displaced Frame Difference) measures how well the current motion model predicts each pixel's intensity in the next frame:

DFDθ(xᵢ, yᵢ) = I(xᵢ + uᵢ, yᵢ + vᵢ, t+1) − I(xᵢ, yᵢ, t) + ξ

The motion accuracy index essentially measures, over a 3×3 neighborhood, how large the prediction error is relative to the local gradient magnitude. The numerator sums the product of gradient magnitude and DFD over the neighborhood — capturing both the reliability of the measurement (large gradients are more informative) and the size of the error. The denominator normalizes by the total gradient energy, with a floor of 9σ² preventing division instability in textureless areas.

The binary weight is then assigned by thresholding:

wᵢ = 1 if |qᵢ| < η // inlier: include in G,d accumulation wᵢ = 0 otherwise // outlier: exclude from G,d accumulation

Pixels with large |qᵢ| (poor fit to the model) are zeroed out of the G matrix, so they cannot bias the motion estimate. This mechanism is what makes the top-down approach work even when regions overlap or labels are imperfect — it robustly isolates the dominant motion within each region.

Incremental Estimation & Hierarchical Processing

Incremental refinement

Rather than estimating θ from scratch each time, the algorithm computes an incremental update Δθ. It warps the next frame using the current model, measures residuals at the warped positions, and solves for a correction. This Δθ is added to the existing model. Repeating this process converges rapidly toward the optimum, analogous to Newton's method. The gradients and DFD are recomputed at the warped positions each iteration, so the linearization stays accurate as the estimate improves.

Image pyramid (hierarchical processing)

Large motions (many pixels per frame) violate the small-displacement assumption behind gradient-based estimation. To handle them, the algorithm builds an image pyramid — for example 3 levels: Level 2 at 160×120, Level 1 at 320×240, Level 0 at 640×480 (full resolution). At the coarsest level, a 20-pixel motion appears as only 5 pixels; the estimate propagates down to finer levels for refinement. At each level the estimation iterates multiple times (typically 2).

Fig. — Image pyramid with 3 hierarchy levels. Each level iterates twice; the estimate propagates coarse → fine.

The PSM algorithm flow

The specific estimation variant used is called the PSM (Parametric Segmentation Model) algorithm. In its conventional form, it first runs motion model computation across all hierarchy levels (with pyramid-level iterations), then runs weight computation across all hierarchy levels, and repeats this outer loop. This structure means the model and weights only interact at the outer loop boundary — limiting convergence speed.

04 — Step 2

Boundary Update

With the motion models estimated, the algorithm must decide which label to assign to every pixel — especially near region boundaries where two motion patterns meet. This is posed as a Markov Random Field (MRF) energy minimization.

The MRF Energy Function

For each pixel at position i, the algorithm evaluates an energy U for every candidate label l and picks the one that minimizes it:

l* = arg min_l U(l, θₗ, I, J, m, m̃) U = U₁(θₗ, I, J) + U₂(l, m) + U₃(l, m, m̃)

This is a local optimization: each pixel chooses independently based on its neighborhood. The three energy terms balance motion fit, spatial smoothness, and temporal consistency.

The Three Energy Terms in Detail

U₁ — Motion Fitting (Data Term)

How well does this pixel match the candidate region's motion?

U₁ is derived from the motion accuracy index qᵢ — the same quantity used for outlier rejection in Step 1 — but now computed using the candidate label's motion model θₗ. If the pixel's brightness change closely matches what model θₗ predicts (small DFD), U₁ is low. If there's a large displaced frame difference, U₁ is high. This is the data term — it measures the physical plausibility of assigning label l to this pixel.

The computation requires: (1) warping the pixel using the candidate model θₗ, (2) reading the next-frame pixel at the warped location via bilinear interpolation, (3) computing the DFD, and (4) evaluating qᵢ over the 3×3 neighborhood. This means the accuracy index hardware is shared between Step 1 and Step 2.

U₂ — Spatial Continuity (Smoothness Prior)

Do neighboring pixels share this label?

U₂ examines the 8 neighbors of pixel i in the current label map m. The more neighbors that carry label l, the lower U₂ becomes. If l would create an isolated island surrounded by different labels, U₂ is high. This is the classic Ising/Potts MRF smoothness prior — it penalizes label discontinuities and ensures region boundaries are spatially coherent rather than noisy.

In hardware, this requires a line buffer to access the row above and the pixel to the left, enabling the 3×3 neighborhood lookup in a single-pass raster scan.

U₃ — Temporal Continuity (Prediction Prior)

Does this label match the prediction from the previous frame?

U₃ penalizes changing the label from what the prediction map m̃ suggests. If the candidate label l equals the predicted label at this position, U₃ is zero; otherwise a penalty is added. This provides temporal stability — labels don't randomly flip between frames in areas where motion estimation is ambiguous or gradients are weak.

This term is essentially a temporal version of U₂: while U₂ enforces spatial consistency with neighbors in the current frame, U₃ enforces consistency with the same position in the previous frame's prediction.

The U₂ and U₃ terms together form the statistical regularization. They are critical in textureless areas (flat walls, sky, road surfaces) where luminance gradients are weak and U₁ alone cannot distinguish between candidate labels. In these regions, the spatial and temporal context "fill in" the correct label based on surrounding evidence.

Multi-scale processing: Boundary update also operates hierarchically — from coarse to fine. At coarse levels, the smoothness prior has a large receptive field relative to the image, establishing rough region shapes. At fine levels, precise boundary placement is refined. This multi-scale MRF approach is critical for accurately segmenting both large and small regions.
05 — Step 3

New Region Detection

Step 2 refines boundaries between known regions. But what about objects that appear for the first time — a car entering the frame, or a previously occluded surface being revealed? These pixels do not match any existing motion model, and Step 3 identifies them.

Static vs. Mobile Classification

For each pixel within a region, the algorithm evaluates the DFD against that region's motion model:

Per-Pixel Decision

Does this pixel's motion match its region, or is it anomalous?

Match (static): The DFD is small — the pixel moves according to the region's model. It keeps its current label.

No match (mobile): The DFD is large — this pixel's actual motion differs significantly from the region's model. It is flagged as a potential new-region pixel.

The decision uses an energy function similar to boundary update, but the candidate labels are different: instead of choosing among existing neighbor labels, the choice is between "keep current label" (static) and "assign to new region" (mobile). The energy function still includes spatial and temporal regularization, so isolated noisy pixels are not incorrectly flagged as new regions.

Clusters of adjacent "mobile" pixels that form spatially coherent groups are assigned a new label, creating a new entry in the Region Table. These new regions will receive their own motion model estimation in the next iteration, allowing the algorithm to progressively discover and track new objects as they appear.

Fig. — New region detection process. Left: a labeled region k with an embedded object moving differently (blue arrows). Center: pixels whose motion vectors differ from region k's model are highlighted (blue). Right: those pixels are classified as "mobile" (gray), forming a candidate new region.
Structural similarity to Step 2: The flowchart for new region detection is identical to boundary update except for the energy function coefficients and the candidate labels. This similarity is what allows the proposed algorithm to unify both into a single "region labeling" operation.
06 — Step 4

Region Prediction

After the label map m(t) is finalized and the motion models θ are known, Step 4 generates a prediction map m̃(t+1) for the next time step.

Label Warping

Each pixel's label is warped forward according to its region's motion model: if pixel (x, y) has label L with model θₗ, then position (x + u, y + v) in the next frame is predicted to also have label L. This creates the prediction map that initializes the next frame's boundary update.

Handling Special Cases

Fig. — Region prediction. The label map e(t−1) is warped using each region's motion model. Region R₂ shifts right by 1 pixel. Red pixels are "uncovered" (revealed when the foreground moves), green pixels are "occlusions" (where labels overlap).
Uncovered Regions

Areas revealed when foreground moves away

When a foreground region moves, the area it previously occupied becomes visible for the first time. These positions receive no warped label and are marked as "uncovered" — a special initialization that signals to the next frame's processing that these pixels need fresh labeling.

Occlusions

Areas where regions overlap after warping

When two regions' warped labels map to the same position, the foreground label takes priority. The occluded background pixels are overwritten.

Region Merging & Cleanup

Post-prediction maintenance

During raster-scan processing, the algorithm detects when multiple new regions (created in Step 3) that originated from the same parent are now spatially adjacent. These are merged by updating the Region Table — the absorbed region is invalidated and its corrected label is set to the surviving region's number. Regions whose pixel count drops below a minimum threshold are deleted.

Fig. — Left: prediction map ẽ(t) showing uncovered pixels (red) and occluded pixels (green) after warping. Right: the corresponding label map e(t−1) with regions R₁ and R₂.

The prediction map is written to external memory and becomes the m̃ input when the next frame pair is processed. This feedback loop gives the algorithm temporal memory — regions grow, refine, and track objects across many frames, building up accurate segmentation over time even from a simple all-background initialization.

07 — Proposed Algorithm

Key Innovations for Pixel-Level Pipelining

Fig. — Conventional algorithm and architecture. Left: loop structures for motion model estimation (top) and region labeling (bottom) with separate hierarchical processing. Right: block diagram with two pipeline stages and double-buffered memories. Bottom-right: timing diagram showing pipelined processing of segments A, B.

The conventional algorithm processes the four stages as large, separate blocks — first running motion model estimation with its own hierarchical loops, then boundary update across the whole image, then new region detection. This creates two problems: the motion model and label map are exchanged only once, limiting convergence speed, and the sequential structure resists hardware pipelining.

The proposed algorithm restructures everything around three changes:

Change 1 — Loop Restructuring

Conventional Loop

  • Motion model computation across all hierarchy levels
  • Then weight computation across all hierarchy levels
  • Repeat above 2× (pyramid-level iteration)
  • Then boundary update across all levels
  • Then new region detection across all levels
  • Model ↔ label map exchanged once

Proposed Loop

  • At each hierarchy level, iterate:
  • → model calc + weight calc + boundary update + new region detection
  • Model ↔ label exchange at every image-unit iteration
  • Frequent exchange → faster convergence
  • Fewer total iterations needed
  • Lower total computation
Fig. — Proposed algorithm loop structure. All four operations (motion model, weight, boundary update, new region detection) are interleaved at each hierarchy level, with image-unit iterations. This enables frequent model↔label exchange and faster convergence.

The fundamental change is moving the interleaving granularity from "after all hierarchy levels" to "after each hierarchy-level image." This means updated labels immediately influence the next motion estimation iteration, and updated models immediately improve the next labeling pass.

Change 2 — Shared Preprocessing

In the conventional algorithm, both motion model estimation and boundary update/new region detection independently compute luminance gradients (Ix, Iy, It) and the motion accuracy index qᵢ. The proposed algorithm computes them once as a shared preprocessing step. This halves the gradient computation cost and — critically — allows a single pixel stream to feed both paths.

One key subtlety enables this sharing: the motion accuracy index used for region labeling uses the motion model from the previous iteration, not the current one being estimated. This one-iteration delay breaks the circular data dependency (model → accuracy → label → model) and enables pure streaming. The pixel data can flow through both the model-estimation path and the labeling path without waiting for the new model to be computed. In practice, since the motion model mostly converges within the first iteration at the finest hierarchy level, this delayed model causes negligible accuracy loss.

Change 3 — Unified Region Labeling

Boundary update and new region detection are structurally near-identical: both evaluate an MRF energy function using the motion accuracy index and neighboring labels, differing only in energy coefficients and candidate label sets. The proposed algorithm unifies them per pixel:

B
Boundary pixel (neighbors have mixed labels)

→ Perform boundary update: evaluate candidate labels from adjacent regions, pick minimum energy.

I
Interior pixel (all neighbors have the same label)

→ Perform new region detection: test whether motion fits current region or should be flagged as "mobile."

This per-pixel branch means both operations happen in a single pass through the image, eliminating the second complete scan. Combined with shared preprocessing, the entire chain — gradient → accuracy → weight → moment accumulation / labeling — becomes a continuous pixel-by-pixel pipeline where one pixel enters and one decision exits every clock cycle.

Convergence Speed & Accuracy

The foreground building (outlined in white/orange) is fully segmented by frame 15 in the proposed method, while the conventional method has not achieved this even at frame 25. Driving Sequence — Vehicle-Mounted Camera

Better accuracy on complex scenes

Conventional method: vehicle not segmented at frame 1.

The proposed method achieves this with fewer total operations — the conventional method iterates over the entire image pyramid twice per frame, while the proposed method's interleaved structure avoids that overhead. At the same clock frequency, the proposed algorithm needs only 62 MHz for VGA 60 fps while the conventional requires 167 MHz for VGA 30 fps.

08 — Architecture

Pixel Pipeline Hardware Architecture

The VLSI architecture directly mirrors the proposed algorithm's streaming structure. All stages form a single pixel-level pipeline with a throughput of 1 pixel per clock cycle (with brief stalls only at region boundaries for context switching, ~4 cycles).

Fig. — Block diagram of the proposed pixel-pipeline architecture.
Fig. — Proposed pixel-pipeline architecture (from presentation). The entire processing chain forms a single pixel-level pipeline from Cache AG through gradient and weight computation, branching into gradient moment calculation (model path) and region labeling (label path).

Key Hardware Blocks

Cache Address Generator (Cache AG)

Reads labels in raster-scan order from external memory, looks up the corresponding region's motion model from MMT0, computes warped destination coordinates via the affine equation (u = a₁+a₂x+a₃y, v = a₄+a₅x+a₆y), and generates read addresses into the next-image cache. The next-image cache (NIC) stores 25 rows (current ± 12) across 16 memory banks, enabling simultaneous readout of a 4×4 pixel neighborhood for sub-pixel bilinear interpolation.

Gradient Calculation

Performs bilinear interpolation at sub-pixel precision to generate the warped pixel value and its neighbors. From these next-frame values and the current-frame values, it computes Ix, Iy (spatial gradients) and It (temporal gradient). In hardware, It is clipped to the range [−128, +127] at 8-bit precision.

Accuracy Index & Weight Calculation

Computes qᵢ over a 3×3 neighborhood (requiring 2 line buffers). The division in qᵢ is implemented as Newton's-method reciprocal with 3 iterations, pipelined at 1 iteration per pipeline stage. The resulting qᵢ has 5-bit precision (1 integer, 4 fractional). The weight wᵢ is a single bit.

Gradient Moment Calculation

Accumulates the G matrix (28 unique elements, since G is symmetric) and d vector (7 elements) per region. The circuit is pipelined and computes all elements in parallel for each pixel. At region boundaries, the current region's G/d are saved to on-chip memory (Gd memory: 8 banks × 512 words × 32 bits) and the next region's are restored — a context switch taking ~4 cycles. Elements are 32-bit fixed-point during accumulation, with rounding applied based on the region's pixel count to prevent overflow for large regions.

Motion Model Calculation (Inverse Matrix)

After each hierarchy-level image is fully scanned, this block computes G⁻¹ via Gauss-Jordan elimination using 40-bit floating-point (32-bit mantissa, 8-bit exponent). The pivot reciprocal is precomputed in parallel with the current elimination step using Newton's method, hiding its latency. The inverse matrix computation takes 444 cycles per region; the model multiplication takes 57 cycles. For 32 regions, this adds modest overhead compared to the pixel-scanning time.

Region Labeling

Evaluates U = U₁+U₂+U₃ for each candidate label using the accuracy index and neighboring labels (from a line buffer). The left-neighbor label update triggers a U₂ correction on-the-fly. Picks the minimum-energy label (9-bit energy value) and writes to the output label map.

Region Prediction

Runs once per frame after all hierarchy iterations. Warps labels forward using MMT1, merges fragmented regions via RT1, counts per-region pixel areas, and deletes tiny regions. An optimization: the prediction at the bottom hierarchy level uses the 1st-iteration model (not 2nd), eliminating a redundant 3rd iteration and saving ~40% of bottom-level cycles. Labels are corrected online during the next frame by referencing RT, avoiding a separate prediction-map rewrite pass.

09 — VLSI Results

Implementation & Performance

The processor was fabricated in a Rohm 0.18 µm 5-metal CMOS process. Circuit description was done in Verilog HDL; verification used both RTL simulation with test images and the EVE Zebu-XXL emulator. Physical LSI testing confirmed identical output to simulation.

At VGA 60 fps, the required clock is only 62 MHz — well below the max 94 MHz, leaving headroom for 91 fps. The conventional architecture needed 167 MHz for just VGA 30 fps. At the same clock, the proposed design delivers over 5× throughput.

Cycle Count Breakdown (VGA 60 fps, 3 levels, 2 iterations, 32 regions)

Level 2 (160×120): 88,540 cycles Level 1 (320×240): 221,758 cycles Level 0 (640×480): 718,622 cycles ─────────────────────────────── Total: 1,028,920 cycles / frame Required freq: 62 MHz for 60 fps

The design also achieves a smaller footprint because:

✓
No frame-size internal image memory

The unified pixel pipeline shares pixel and label reads, eliminating the need to buffer entire segmented images (which the conventional design required).

✓
Shared gradient & accuracy circuits

Computing these once instead of independently in each stage roughly halves the logic for these functions.

✓
Unified boundary update + new region detection

A single labeling circuit handles both, reducing duplicated energy-computation hardware.

Target application: Automotive safety driver assistance using stereo video — where real-time segmentation of moving vehicles, pedestrians, and obstacles at high frame rates is critical for collision avoidance. Parameters (hierarchy levels, iteration count, etc.) are configurable via internal register writes.
